title: AI Just Made History in the Middle of a Meltdown
dek: AI may have just cracked the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most storied problems in mathematics, in the same week Jensen Huang was reinstated at Nvidia with the President's thumb on the scale and Anthropic's IPO drew a backlash. Historic capability and a narrative meltdown are arriving at the same time.

oneIdea.headline: AI is making history while its narrative melts down.
oneIdea.summary: In basically every way, we're entering a new phase of AI. An Anthropic mathematician working with Claude has claimed a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and the labs are already circling P vs NP. Meanwhile Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia because President Trump personally intervened, which turns a tech-and-China scandal into a potential corruption scandal. Anthropic's record IPO is being cast as a cynical liquidity grab. The fight to return Jensen may be over, but the battle to recover the AI narrative has barely begun.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: A result nobody can read
items.body: The claimed proof runs to seventeen million lines of machine-checkable code that no mathematician can follow, and its own author says it may be wrong. Medicine will meet the same problem: an answer that is checkable by machine but not understood by any person. For now our rule should hold. If no accountable clinician can explain why a recommendation is right, it is not ready to act on.

items.title: Unverified is unverified
items.body: NLW is careful to call this a historic claim and not a settled fact; some already report errors in the code. Zitron ignores it. Treat it as we would an exciting preprint from a company with a product to sell, announced the week after its flotation: interesting, possibly important, and awaiting independent confirmation.

items.title: Models whose reasoning cannot be seen
items.body: A smaller item matters more for us. New model designs do their reasoning internally and no longer show a trace of it. For clinical safety that removes one of the few ways to audit why a tool said what it said. When a supplier changes model, ask whether the reasoning is still inspectable. Otherwise this edition has little direct clinical relevance.

the_other_side.text: Zitron, writing the same day, would say the industry's problem is not its narrative but its finances. He argues the President forced Huang's return to steady the stock market, and that an industry needing that is brittle. He calls Anthropic's flotation "exit liquidity for its founders, staff and VCs", noting the shares have slid back towards the offer price and that many more will become tradeable within six months. He says token spending has plateaued and prices are falling. He does not mention the claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether the industry's trouble is one of reputation or of solvency. Both accept as fact that the President intervened in Huang's reinstatement, that Anthropic's shares sit only just above their offer price, and that its founders sold stock. The empirical question is whether the money holds; the observable is whether Anthropic stays above its eighty-three dollar offer price through the end of the lock-up, and what its first accounts show. The residue is worldview: whether a striking result in mathematics tells you anything about a business. For Whittemore to be vindicated, the proof must survive checking and capability gains must turn into revenue while the politics is managed. For Zitron, the shares must break the offer price and funding tighten, whatever the models can do. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both describe the flotation as widely seen as a sale by insiders. Watch the offer price and the lock-up expiry.

headlines.headline: I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.
headlines.summary: He says the method extends to the generalized Riemann hypothesis and, with more time, likely the extended version too. He also reflected on what the result means: "It is natural to feel that this is an end... but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me" that he believes it signals something far greater across science.

headlines.headline: Why the Riemann hypothesis is such a big deal
headlines.summary: Proposed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, it holds that the apparently random gaps between prime numbers actually follow a pattern. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a million-dollar prize attached, and for many mathematicians it has been "the sacred object" since childhood.

headlines.headline: The proof was held back until after Anthropic's IPO
headlines.summary: Alpoge was satisfied with the work by the prior Sunday and raised disclosure with Dario Amodei during IPO week. They waited, and he called the timing "horrible." The proof was published only in Lean, runs to 17 million lines, isn't readable even by top mathematicians, and Alpoge acknowledged it could be false.

headlines.headline: Mathematicians split over a proof no human can fully understand
headlines.summary: The Lean community declared "full confidence" the proof is correct. The Association for Human Mathematics countered that no human can reasonably claim to be responsible for or understand the document, and called it a corporate model of proof production that asks scientists to entrust research to machines AI companies control.

headlines.headline: Just last month, Terence Tao thought this was decades away
headlines.summary: In a Numberphile video, the Fields medalist said the AI companies had surely thrown more effort at Riemann than they disclosed and "couldn't touch it." He guessed humans and AIs together might make progress around 2050. He had earlier said a problem like this probably needs a new type of mathematics to be created.

headlines.headline: P vs NP becomes the final boss, maybe not for long
headlines.summary: Scott Aaronson wrote that P vs NP now moves firmly into place as the last great problem standing, then asked how much longer anything we take for granted will last. On Monday, both Anthropic and OpenAI published limited proofs related to P vs NP.

headlines.headline: Don't treat it as rock-solid yet
headlines.summary: A Lean proof is just as fallible as any other computer program, and some people claim to have found bugs in the Riemann code. Until there is additional verification, the result is a historic claim, not a settled fact.

headlines.headline: A mathematical wormhole no human would build
headlines.summary: Abhishek Saha of Queen Mary University of London described the approach as "not theory building in the usual sense": a 25,000-page tour through existing infrastructure with no obvious connection to the goal. He credited the human collaborator too, saying no current AI could do this alone either. Aaron Levie's takeaway is that solving problems is about to look very different.

headlines.headline: Inside SpaceX AI: 'Sell Compute Because We Can't Compete'
headlines.summary: The New York Times reports Musk told employees SpaceX is falling behind in AI, so renting compute to rivals pays better than using it. He shares data on Grok's lag in a group chat of hundreds of engineers, made people itemize GPU use, and renamed the chat "Sell Compute Because We Can't Compete." The Times framed SpaceX as a neo-cloud tied to Anthropic's GPU demand, not a frontier lab.

headlines.headline: The only thing that matters for competitiveness is revenue per GPU, not benchmarks.
headlines.attribution: Elon Musk, in an internal SpaceX group chat, per The New York Times
headlines.summary: Musk followed up in the group chat: "If you can't pay for your GPUs, then you either go bankrupt or you become a computer rental company." He also warned that anyone wasting GPUs while the company is failing to compete would be asked to leave.

headlines.headline: Digital Optimus stalls
headlines.summary: SpaceX spent the fall building a knowledge-worker agent with Tesla engineers, initially trained on video games like Diablo and League of Legends. Musk was reportedly unhappy with the pace, and the Tesla engineers were moved to Grok model training. There's no real bombshell here, but it shows Grok isn't going anywhere fast.

headlines.headline: SpaceX's AI hopes rest on keeping the Cursor team
headlines.summary: The Pragmatic Engineer's author called it an open secret that the Cursor team is SpaceX's only strong model-building group and that the company struggles to hire top-lab talent. His argument: Cursor was a place people wanted to join, while SpaceX is a place where the CEO calls the shots.

headlines.headline: GLM 5.4 bets on looped transformers
headlines.summary: ZAI says looped transformers, where reasoning happens inside the model weights rather than in output tokens, let a 750B-parameter model match a 2–3T-parameter one, claiming Kimi 3.1-level performance without ultra-large inference costs. It also touts "generalized coding": code as the foundation for broad tasks, shown off with a music video built entirely in code. There are no benchmarks yet, which many read as a bad sign.

headlines.headline: The loopers are coming. Observability be damned?
headlines.summary: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini is also looped, and analysts expect more looped models within three to four months, with open labs potentially making an Astra-like jump at 2–3T parameters. The cost is that users lose the full reasoning trace. Semi Analysis expects that safety question to kick off the next phase of the open-model wars.

headlines.headline: Jensen is back. That doesn't mean it's over
headlines.summary: Huang returned to applause and promised to be "a better CEO the second time around." As Sam Altman learned in 2023, things never fully return to normal after a reinstatement, and Jensen's road may be even harder. This is only the opening act.

headlines.headline: I gave them enough assurance.
headlines.summary: In an hour-long CNBC call-in, Trump said he convinced the Nvidia board to bring Jensen back "for the country." Asked whether he told them Jensen wouldn't be prosecuted, this was his answer. He also said Huang would not have been reinstated without him.

headlines.headline: Trump called into the board meeting because of the market
headlines.summary: Semafor and CNN confirmed Trump personally called into the board meeting after a weekend pressure campaign with JD Vance. CNN reports he had been "stewing for days" over the stock-market sell-off. The White House made no secret of it: "President Trump was totally involved."

headlines.headline: Outside tech, the public isn't buying the celebration
headlines.summary: Tech leaders cheered on X, but a YouGov poll found 54% of Americans think Huang's affair definitely or probably compromised national security, including 61% of Republicans. Newt Gingrich called on Congress to treat it as a national security issue of enormous proportions.

headlines.headline: Trump turned a China scandal into a corruption scandal
headlines.summary: 56% of voters this month said AI and data centers were a major factor in their vote, and 90% said the same of corruption, the top issue ahead of cost of living. By intervening so overtly, the president made this about Jensen's ties to Trump as well as his ties to China, and handed Congress fresh ammunition.

headlines.headline: Washington is lining up, from both parties
headlines.summary: Jensen testifies before Senate Banking next Thursday, and he and Nvidia's general counsel face closed-door interviews before that. Hakeem Jeffries promised a wide-ranging probe into Nvidia and the Commerce Department. Three Republican national-security chairs said the board's brief investigation doesn't erase the questions. Some on the right expect this to become an impeachment issue once Democrats take Congress.

headlines.headline: Commerce blacklists Megaspeed, removing all wiggle room
headlines.summary: The Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its list over the risk of diverting advanced computing goods to unauthorized end users. The administration now officially treats it as a smuggling risk, which makes it easy for critics to ask why Lutnick didn't act when the deal was approved back in March.

headlines.headline: The rally Trump wanted, partly
headlines.summary: Nvidia closed up 31.5% and the Nasdaq 100 rose 6.9%. Nvidia has recovered its post-ouster losses but is still 30% below its October high. The Nasdaq remains 4.3% below where it was at the resignation and 14.3% below its all-time high, with months of hearings ahead.

headlines.headline: Anthropic is flirting with its IPO price as the backlash grows
headlines.summary: Anthropic missed the rally, fell another 1.4%, and closed just $4 above its IPO price, a level that could trigger forced institutional selling if broken. The Guardian estimates each of the seven co-founders is worth $20B and 600 employees are worth more than $100M each. Filings confirm each co-founder sold $2B in shares, fueling the charge that the IPO was an exit-liquidity grab.

headlines.headline: Why this fight has legs: nine or ten reasonable lenses
headlines.summary: Executive accountability and double standards, media hit-jobism, cronyism, "number go up" economics, state-capitalist intervention, open vs. closed source. Even people who put national security first disagree: some say chips reaching China help China, others say they hurt it. Any of these can reasonably be the most important to a given person, so the story won't settle.

headlines.headline: The battle to recover the AI narrative has barely begun
headlines.summary: Jensen faces months of grueling hearings, Trump has tied himself tightly to the scandal, and the first-ever retail access to a frontier lab is being cast as a cynical liquidity grab. The fight to return Jensen may be over, but the narrative war is just starting.
